oneliner.t: Hoover Republican who has represented Alabama's 6th District since January 2015, chairs the Energy and Commerce oversight subcommittee, and co-founded the Alabama Policy Institute think tank.

born.t: May 14, 1954, Hackleburg, Alabama (Wikipedia); Ballotpedia gives the birthplace as Haleyville, Alabama — the two sources disagree on the town.

hometown.t: Grew up on a 40-acre family farm in northwest Alabama (Hackleburg per Wikipedia; Haleyville per Ballotpedia)

upbringing.t: Wikipedia says he grew up on a 40-acre farm where he helped tend the garden and animals, was the first in his family to earn a college degree, and was a walk-on wide receiver at the University of Alabama under Bear Bryant. He co-founded the Alabama Family Alliance in 1989 (later renamed the Alabama Policy Institute), led it for about 25 years until 2014, and helped found the State Policy Network. The farm, first-in-family and walk-on details rest on Wikipedia alone in this research.

career.org: Alabama Family Alliance / Alabama Policy Institute (state think tank)

platform.t: Supports gun rights, including interstate concealed carry.
Supports abortion restrictions; backed the 2022 overturning of Roe v. Wade.
Opposes illegal immigration and supports deportations.
Says the goal is keeping GOP control of the House and Senate and "finishing the job President Trump started."

promises.t: Help keep Republican majorities in the House and Senate and finish the job President Trump started (Aug 11, 2026 primary-night statement).

claims.claim: Co-founded the Alabama Policy Institute (founded 1989 as the Alabama Family Alliance) and led it for about 25 years.

said.where: Biography as reported (BirminghamWatch, Wikipedia); campaign about page unreachable

record.t: Two independent references agree he co-founded API; Wikipedia dates the founding to 1989 and his presidency to 2014.

claims.claim: Holds a degree in operations management from the University of Alabama.

said.where: Biography as reported (Ballotpedia, Wikipedia); campaign about page unreachable

record.t: Ballotpedia (1977) and Wikipedia both list a University of Alabama operations-management degree; no registrar record checked.

claims.claim: Was a walk-on wide receiver for Alabama under Bear Bryant and the first in his family to earn a college degree.

said.where: Biography as reported (Wikipedia); campaign about page unreachable

record.t: Only one secondary source (Wikipedia) was reached; no roster or other record checked.

claims.claim: In 2014 he said he would serve only 10 years in Congress.

said.where: 2014 campaign (as reported by Alabama Reflector and Wikipedia)

record.t: He said in 2014 he would serve no more than five terms (10 years) and acknowledged that pledge in 2023. He sought a sixth term in 2024 and is the 2026 nominee for a seventh. Separately, U.S. Term Limits faulted him in 2021 for not co-sponsoring its constitutional amendment; he said he had "prayed for God to give me clarity" and disputes how the group describes the pledge's scope.

claims.note: Same fact as the term-limits said-vs-did entry; counted once in honesty.

claims.claim: "I didn't go to Washington to be a celebrity."

said.where: Shelby County GOP remarks, reported by BirminghamWatch

record.t: A self-characterization, not a checkable fact.

claims.claim: District residents are "hardworking, faithful, and conservative to the core."

said.where: Primary-night statement, reported by Alabama Reflector

record.t: A characterization. For context, he won 70.3% in 2024, and every listed forecaster rates AL-06 Safe/Solid R.

claims.claim: Led the Alabama Policy Institute think tank.

said.where: 2014 campaign site 'Meet Gary' page, as summarized in Ballotpedia's biography (campaign page accessed by Ballotpedia 2014-02-11). palmerforalabama.com could not be opened.

record.t: He co-founded the Alabama Family Alliance in 1989, which became the Alabama Policy Institute. He was its president for about 25 years and stepped down in 2014 to run for Congress. BirminghamWatch also identifies him as an API co-founder.

claims.claim: House and Senate Republicans have worked to save money and lower costs (reporter's paraphrase).

said.where: remarks to the Shelby County Republican group, as reported by BirminghamWatch (article date)

record.t: The main 2025 GOP fiscal law, P.L. 119-21 (H.R. 1), which Palmer voted for (Roll Call 190), cuts direct spending by about $1.1 trillion over 2025–2034. CBO estimates it also cuts revenue by about $4.5 trillion, for a net deficit increase of about $3.4 trillion. Spending was cut, but the law does not save money on net. 'Lower costs' is too general to check.

said.t: Said he would serve no more than five terms (10 years); acknowledged the pledge in 2023.

did.t: Ran for a sixth term in 2024 and is the 2026 GOP nominee for a seventh.
Voted Nay on H.R. 1834, the three-year extension of enhanced ACA premium tax credits (passed 230–196).

said.t: His 2014 campaign site listed concern about the national debt.

did.t: Voted Nay on the 2023 Fiscal Responsibility Act (CBO: about $1.5T in deficit reduction over 2023–2033) and Yea on H.R. 1 in 2025 (CBO: about $3.4T added to deficits over 2025–2034). A stated debt concern can support either vote; the record is mixed on deficit effect.

promises_prev.promise: Serve no more than 10 years in Congress.

evidence.t: Sought re-election in 2024 (beyond 10 years) and won the 2026 GOP nomination.

complicating.t: He publicly said he had clarity from God to run again; U.S. Term Limits criticized the reversal.

entries.t: Sought a sixth term; running for a seventh in 2026.

aipac_endorse.t: Not confirmed — Track AIPAC shows no AIPAC-endorsement label for him (as of 2026-10-08); AIPAC's own endorsement page was not checked.

aipac_pac.note: 2023–2024 cycle only: FEC-itemized receipts from 'American Israel Public Affairs Committee PAC' (AIPAC PAC conduit), $5,000 on 2024-10-14 plus small April 2024 entries, as summed from ProPublica's Itemizer listing. Other cycles not checked.

others.name: All pro-Israel PACs and their large donors (Track AIPAC career total; lists AIPAC, AMP, AGG, MDACC, RJC, USI)

votes.bill: H.R. 8034 Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act
votes.what: About $26 billion in emergency funding for Israel's missile defense, U.S. regional operations and humanitarian aid including for Gaza (CBO ~$26.4B); passed 366–58 and later enacted inside H.R. 815.
Directs the Education Department to use the IHRA working definition of antisemitism in Title VI enforcement; passed 320–91, not taken up by the Senate.

votes.bill: H.R. 23 Illegitimate Court Counteraction Act (ICC sanctions)
votes.what: Would require sanctions on International Criminal Court officials who investigate or prosecute U.S. or allied (including Israeli) protected persons; passed 243–140.

fec.history_note: Cycles 2018 and 2020 were not retrieved (FEC pages returned HTTP 429 rate limits). In the documented cycles, PAC ('other committee') money ran from about 14% of receipts (2014) to about 44% (2026 to date). 'other' in 2026 = $32,149.97 in transfers from authorized (joint fundraising) committees plus $7,284.40 in offsets. Business vs. ideological PAC split not computed (OpenSecrets blocked; FEC itemized receipts load by script). Outside spending: no independent expenditures for or against him turned up in the sources reached; FEC independent-expenditure data was not checked directly.

corp.t: Business and trade PAC money every documented cycle. FEC 'other committee' contributions were $260,300 (2014), $285,264 (2016), $410,795 (2022), $596,510 (2024) and $464,000 (2025–Jul 22, 2026; about 44% of receipts). ProPublica's 2023–24 itemized list shows Alabama Farmers Federation $10,000, Koch Inc. $7,500, National Association of Realtors $7,000, Protective Life, Vulcan Materials, Drummond Co. and Regions Financial $5,000 each, and Verizon and AT&T $3,000 each. Several are in sectors under his Energy and Commerce committee: coal, materials and telecom. Earliest found: Alabama Retail Association PAC, $500, Sept 16, 2014. Wikipedia, citing a 2023 CoinDesk report, says he received FTX-linked money.

lobby.t: Track AIPAC lists $88,031 in career donations from pro-Israel PACs (AIPAC, AMP, AGG, MDACC, RJC, USI) and their large donors, and $0 in independent expenditures. FEC-itemized receipts from the AIPAC PAC conduit total $5,012 in 2023–24, including $5,000 on Oct 14, 2024.

note.t: 2025 annual report (filed Apr 15, 2026). Holdings are mostly diversified ETFs (OneAscent, Vanguard Treasury, Eventide) and a Schwab money-market fund in his IRA, his spouse's IRA and a joint account. Other holdings: a 22.2% interest in Canaan LLC timberland near Vernon, AL ($250K–$500K), a variable annuity, and small joint positions in AT&T and Warner Bros. Discovery, both telecom/media companies in Energy and Commerce's jurisdiction. All 32 transactions in 2025 were money-fund or ETF trades, mainly an Oct 8, 2025 reallocation; none were individual stocks. No liabilities, no foreign assets, no outside positions. The spouse has part-time hourly earned income. The range sums asset brackets; the AT&T row's value was read as $15,001–$50,000 because the PDF text splits it. The personal residence is not reportable and is excluded.

committees: Energy and Commerce (Chair, Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee; Energy; Environment)
Oversight and Government Reform (Economic Growth, Energy Policy and Regulatory Affairs; Government Operations)

revolving.role: Former chief of staff, now a registered lobbyist
revolving.t: Quiver Quantitative's lobbying-disclosure summary lists one former Palmer staffer, Terry Allen (described as chief of staff), as a lobbyist for one client, Will Technology Inc. Latest filing: Apr 9, 2026. Not checked against Senate LDA records (blocked).

democracy.t: Not among the House members who rose to object to 2016 electoral votes. Every objection that day was ruled out of order for lacking a senator's signature, and there was no recorded vote.
Signed the House Republican amicus brief supporting Texas v. Pennsylvania, the suit seeking to overturn 2020 results in four states. The Supreme Court declined to hear it.
Voted Yea on the objection to Arizona's electoral votes (Roll Call 10; failed 121–303).
Voted Yea on the objection to Pennsylvania's electoral votes (Roll Call 11; failed 138–282).
Said Donald Trump bore blame for 'sending' the attackers to the Capitol, then voted against the second impeachment.

note.t: Raised in northwest Alabama (Marion/Winston County area, outside AL-06). Has lived and worked in the Birmingham area for decades: API is Birmingham-based and he is a longtime Briarwood Presbyterian member. Years of district residence not documented.

research_notes: BALLOT (independent William Karl Puetz IV): NOT CONFIRMED. On Aug 26, 2026 the Alabama Secretary of State posted one 'State Certification of Independent Candidate' for the 2026 general election, but the PDF is a scanned image with no readable text, so the office and name could not be confirmed. No Puetz reference appears on the SOS page, on Wikipedia's 2026 Alabama House elections page (which lists only Palmer and Mercer as AL-06 nominees), or in the Aug 11–12 Reflector and BirminghamWatch coverage of the Palmer–Mercer matchup. An earlier research note found one Green Papers listing naming him, which conflicts with the Green Papers general-election list. A human should check the scanned certification or call the SOS Elections Division (Jeff Elrod, 334-353-7177). MONEY: FEC figures are from committee C00551374 pages; the candidate page was rate-limited (HTTP 429). Coverage runs through Jul 22, 2026 (Reflector reported the same: raised $1M, spent $946K). Wikipedia's table shows $708,577 raised through Mar 31, 2026. PAC detail is from ProPublica's Itemizer list; amounts were summed by the reading tool from roughly 380 entries, so treat individual PAC totals as approximate. TERMS: 2026 would be his seventh term (first elected 2014). Al-house.json's 'sixth term' label is off by one. EFFECTIVENESS: sponsored/enacted bill counts not available (congress.gov blocked). The Wikipedia article says he added Birmingham Northern Beltline funding to the infrastructure bill but voted against final passage. | 2026-10-08 claims/ethics pass: added 2 claims: led API (true, from the 2014 'Meet Gary' page via Ballotpedia) and 'Republicans worked to save money' (partly, citing CBO's estimate of P.L. 119-21 and Roll Call 190). Checkable-verdict claims now number 5. The 2014 issues-page debt claim ($17.2T) is unrated pending a Treasury source. checklist.ethics changed from 'no' to 'news' (ethics.house.gov unreachable; Wikipedia/Reflector/BirminghamWatch show no House Ethics/OCE matter). Disclosures ('done', 2025 PFD) and democracy ('done', Clerk roll calls 10/11) unchanged. The web-search budget was exhausted, so no further ad or ethics news search was possible.
